editorial.headline: Wholesale Trade in Radioactive Minerals: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the wholesale movement of radioactive minerals and specified uranium and thorium materials, with foreign ownership open nationally up to 100%.
editorial.body:
Wholesale trade in radioactive minerals is a narrowly defined activity with serious material at its centre. It covers the wholesale trade of radioactive minerals including radium, thorium, uranium, monazite and other radioactive mineral substances. Its stated scope also extends to the transfer, export and/or import of uranium ore, thorium ore, concentrated uranium and concentrated thorium. In practical terms, this is the commercial wholesale layer around these named materials: their trade, movement and the specified cross-border transactions set out in the activity description.

The activity is open across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the code is not framed as a category reserved for one business size. A registrant may sit at any of those listed scales, while still remaining within the defined wholesale scope. The operative boundary is therefore the material and transaction description itself: radioactive minerals and the specifically identified ores and concentrates, rather than a generalised minerals-trading label.

At national level, the PMA position is unambiguous. The activity is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. For a foreign-owned enterprise, that means the national ceiling does not require an Indonesian ownership share under this record. The basis cited for that national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. It is a clear national opening, but it should be read alongside Bali’s distinct provincial screening position rather than treated as a substitute for it.

In Bali, this activity is not blocked by the province-wide PMA moratorium described in the record. Bali permanently blocks Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA across the island; this activity sits outside that blocked outcome. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is recorded as Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The honest conclusion is straightforward: a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, subject to the higher-risk position recorded for the Large scale—not because Bali ignores its moratorium, but because this activity is not within the Low or Medium-Low risk group that moratorium blocks.
